lead: Listening seems like the easy part, and it is the rarest. This lesson separates three levels of listening, shows the talk ratio that changes the result, and teaches you to build rapport in a few minutes, without forced friendliness and without turning into someone else. Anyone who advises a company for months needs this from the very first minute.
objetivo: listen on 3 levels, let the client take up most of the conversation, and build rapport in 2 or 3 minutes, without forcing it.

aprende.t: The talk ratio that decides the conversation
The three levels of listening and how to move up one per conversation
Rapport in two or three minutes, and when to stop
The energy you give off while you read the client

hero_alt: Adult man listening carefully in a work conversation, with his hand resting on a notebook.

secoes.sub: From the most common to the rarest. Click each level.

nos.detalhe: You hear the words while you build your answer. Technically you listened; in practice, half your attention was looking for the next argument. It produces polite conversations and lost sales.
You chase the meaning: what is this person telling me? The next question comes from the last answer, not from your list. Here the conversation becomes an investigation.
You listen to the tone, the pauses, and what was left unsaid. A long pause can mean "I'm thinking" or "I checked out five minutes ago," and the right move is the opposite in each case.

secoes.legenda: The easiest level is the most frequent one. Moving up one layer per conversation already changes your month's results.
secoes.dica: Compare two conversations with the same content: in one you talk 80% of the time and leave with hypotheses; in the other the client talks 80% and you leave with facts they told you themselves.

secoes.titulo: How to recognize your level and move up
secoes.sub: A test for level 1, three moves for level 2, and what level 3 picks up.

texto: You interrupt with "exactly!" before the sentence ends. Afterward you remember what you said, not what you heard. You ask the same questions in every conversation.
Honest test: when you hang up, write down from memory three sentences from the client, in their own words. If only what you said comes out, you stayed at level 1.

passos.sub: pull the thread, hand it back, ask about the effect
texto: Pull the thread: "you said this always runs late; how late, usually?". Hand it back in their words: "so the bottleneck isn't the order, it's the checking. Is that right?".
Ask about the effect: "and when it runs late, who feels it first?". The answer reveals who wants this solved the most.

passos.sub: and what gets in the way
texto: The voice that drops on a topic, the sentence that starts and never ends, the subject he changes every time you get close.
What gets in the way: filling every pause, taking so many notes that you stop listening, and interpreting on your own. Confirm with a question, not a guess.

Rapport is the feeling of being in tune. Make a light comment and see if the person gives something back. If they came back with a question, they want to talk; if they answered in one line, they want to work: move on.
Fake rapport ("I have one too!" when you don't) falls apart by the third question and makes the person doubt everything that comes after.

secoes.titulo: Mirror the pace and manage your own energy
secoes.sub: While you read the client, they are reading you.

texto: Fast, upbeat client: match the energy and keep your questions coming. Reserved client: lower your volume and stretch your pauses. Straight-to-the-point client: cut the small talk down to thirty seconds.
Manipulation test: if it would still make sense with the client knowing what you are doing, it is not manipulation.
Knowing what you want from that conversation removes half the anxiety. Without a goal, you improvise, and improvising sounds like insecurity.
If the client is curt, take it in stride and hand back a question. And celebrate on the inside: celebrating a yes too much tells them it is rare for you.
Write down their phrases, numbers and deadlines, not what you felt. A written phrase becomes a proposal the following week; a feeling disappears in two days.

secoes.sub: Practice level 2 without spending a real conversation: the AI plays the difficult client.

blocos.rot: Prompt · listening practice with a simulated client
blocos.conteudo:
You are going to simulate a client so I can practice listening. Rules:
ROLE: you are <owner of a mid-sized trucking company, busy and skeptical>. You have a real problem
with <describe in one line, e.g.: rework when checking orders>, but you will NOT hand it over
on a silver platter: answer briefly, mention symptoms and only go deeper if I ask a good question.
MY TASK: find the root problem and how much it costs, only by asking questions.
SIMULATION RULES:
- One line at a time. Never write my lines.
- If I propose a solution before understanding the problem, resist the way a real client would.
- If I ask two questions in the same message, answer only the second.
AT THE END (when I write "end"): step out of the role and give me a report with
(a) what the root problem was that I should have found,
(b) my questions that worked and why,
(c) the moments when I spoke when I should have waited,
(d) a score from 0 to 10 for my listening, and be tough.

secoes.sub: One real conversation and one practice session.

exercicios.texto: In your next work conversation (sales or not), when you hang up, write from memory three phrases the other person said, in their own words, and estimate your share of the talking.
exercicios.pronto: you have 3 phrases from the other person in quotes, with no paraphrasing, and a number for your share of the talking.

exercicios.texto: Run the simulated client prompt with the type of company you serve. Lead by only asking questions and write "end" when you think you've reached the root.
exercicios.pronto: the final report points out at least 1 moment where you steamrolled; if it only had praise, you redid it asking for harshness.

secoes.sub: 4 questions. The explanation appears after your attempt.

perguntas.p: The client answered your light question with a short sentence and gave nothing back. What does that indicate?
opcoes: That he didn't like you; it's worth pushing on another personal topic
That he wants to get to the point; end the small talk and start the investigation
That the conversation is lost and it's better to reschedule
perguntas.explica: Offer the thread and see if they pull it. A short answer is the sign of someone who wants to work: respect that and move on. Pushing the chat feels forced.

perguntas.p: Which move is typical of listening level 2?
opcoes: Interrupting with "exactly!" to show you understood
Handing it back in their words: "so the bottleneck is the order check, is that right?"
Following the list of questions in the prepared order
perguntas.explica: At level 2 the next question comes from the last answer. Interrupting and following a fixed list are level 1 signs.

perguntas.p: A long pause from the client in the middle of the conversation. What should you do?
opcoes: Fill it right away, so it doesn't get awkward
Wait and, if you need to, confirm with a question what it means
perguntas.explica: A pause can mean "I'm thinking" or "I checked out." Filling it erases the signal before you can read it; confirming with a question avoids guessing.

perguntas.p: Why does celebrating a small yes too much get in the way?
opcoes: Because it signals need: it looks like that is rare for you
Because the client may ask for a discount
perguntas.explica: Too much enthusiasm raises the question "why is no one else buying?" A "great, let's agree on the next steps" signals routine, and routine puts the buyer at ease.

itens.texto: The client takes up most of the time; you leave with facts they said themselves.
Answer, understand and listen to the energy. Move up one level per conversation.
Two to three minutes, and follow the thread only if the person pulls it.
Too much need pushes people away; ease puts them at ease.
